sources.citation: Verstraete, Jean-Christophe. 2022. Pathways of initial consonant loss: A Middle Paman case study. Journal of Historical Linguistics (author ms).
sources.note: Zero mentions of Pakanh; stress discussed only for Umpithamu and Lamalamic.

sources.citation: Sommer, Bruce A. 1969. Kunjen phonology: synchronic and diachronic. Pacific Linguistics B-11. Canberra: ANU. (AIATSIS/ozbib tags Y64 Pakanh; Glottolog 12834)
sources.note: Bakanha appears only in the ethnographic/classificatory survey (pp. 2-3, 8, 14-15: 'Bakanha data were provided by Mrs Lucy Native, Mrs Nancy Gordon, and Mr Frank Yam.. it became evident that Bakanha was not a Kunjen dialect.. a brief study was attempted') and in lexicostatistic tables. All stress statements (nuclear syllable; 'Stress may occur on any of the last three syllables.. frequently stressed on the final syllable') are about Oykangand/Olgol, not Bakanha.

sources.citation: McConnel, Ursula H. 1945. Wikmunkan phonetics. Oceania 15(4): 353-375.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Early phonetic sketch; AIATSIS/ozbib tags it for Pakanh (Y64) among six languages, so it may carry phonetic notes (possibly on stress) for the Coen 'Koko-Jan'/Pakanh material; primarily Wik-Mungkan.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic organisation and native title: the Wik case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press. (Glottolog subclassification source, pp. 80, 103, 129, 139)
sources.note: Nothing on Pakanh stress. Pakanh treated only for classification ('Philip Hamilton has established that Pakanh and Ayapathu.. are genetically part of the Wik Subgroup and are close dialects of a single language', p. 102) and Hale's Pakanh vocabulary L14' 'from Hamilton and Yam 1994' (pp. 173-174).

sources.citation: Hamilton, Philip. 1997 [Glottolog: Hamilton 1998]. Pakanh Phoneme Inventory. 1 p. PDF in: Uw Oykangand and Uw Olkola Multimedia Dictionary (community website, Kowanyama).http://www.oocities.org/athens/delphi/2970/orthopak.pdf
sources.note: Presupposes word stress but gives no placement: 'The long or tense allophones such as [pʰː], [ᵇm], [mː] and [wː] occur following short stressed vowels. The short or lax allophones such as [b], [β], [m] and [w] occur following long stressed vowels.' Nothing on which syllable is stressed.

sources.citation: Hamilton, Philip. 1997. Ayapathu Wordlist, 4 pp. Ms posted athttp://www.oocities.org/athens/delphi/2970/ayapathu.htm(Glottolog 662460; language code note: 'Ayapathu here is Western Ayapathu = Pakanha [pkn]')

Hamilton, Philip. 1997. Pakanh Wordlist (Pakanh Alphabetical Search Index), 41 pp. Ms posted athttp://www.oocities.org/athens/delphi/2970/pakalpha.htm(Glottolog 662461, listed by Glottolog as a wordlist)
sources.note: Nothing; orthographic wordlist without stress marks or phonological notes.

sources.citation: Hamilton, Philip. 1997. Uw Oykangand and Uw Olkola Multimedia Dictionary: site index, 'Uw Olkola and Uw Oykangand information' page, 'Cape York Peninsula' page, Uw Oykangand phoneme inventory PDF.http://www.oocities.org/athens/delphi/2970/
sources.note: Nothing on stress for any of the three languages; Pakanh mentioned only as one of the traditional-owner peoples of the interior Cape.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter. 1978. Wik: Aboriginal society, territory and language at Cape Keerweer, Cape York Peninsula, Australia. PhD thesis, University of Queensland (chapter 'Linguistic Relationships', Glottolog 38870)
sources.note: Nothing on Pakanha; only cites 'Sommer, B.A. n.d.2 Bakanha. Fieldnotes, holograph' and Thompson's wordlist as the Pakanha/Ayapathu sources.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page for Pakanha (paka1251) and Wikipedia 'Pakanha language'
sources.note: Glottolog lists a single descriptive reference (Sonnaert 2013). Wikipedia's phonology section (vowels, 15 consonants) is taken from Hamilton 1998 and says nothing about stress.
